title: Ali El Seblani
text:
HARVEY MUDD COLLEGE — Systems Engineering Practicum Proctor




E79 — Systems Engineering — is a rigorous lab-based course at Harvey Mudd College that uses underwater robotics as a teaching vehicle to introduce students to the systems engineering approach. Students learn to model, construct, analyze, design, and control mechanical, thermal, and electrical systems across 13 hands-on practicums spanning the full semester.

As a Systems Engineering Practicum Proctor, my role is to guide teams of two students through each 2.5-hour practicum session — helping them navigate complex concepts in underwater robotics, circuit design, soldering, and sensor integration. I ensure that students arrive prepared, work collaboratively, and follow strict safety protocols in the lab, including proper handling of electrical components, epoxies, and soldering equipment.

Beyond technical guidance, I serve as a resource for debugging, troubleshooting, and helping students connect theoretical systems engineering concepts to real hands-on challenges. Having built and deployed an underwater ROV myself in E79, I bring firsthand experience to every session — understanding exactly what students are working through and where they are likely to struggle.

GENERAL MOTORS —  Autonomous Robotics Center Manufacturing Engineering Intern
This past summer, I interned at General Motors in the General Assembly department and the Autonomous Robotics Center division in Burton, Michigan as a Manufacturing Engineering Intern. I was directly on the floor of a live processing plant, supporting the launch and integration of an Automated Storage and Retrieval System (ASRS) — a large-scale automation initiative aimed at transforming how materials are stored, retrieved, and delivered across production departments.
My role placed me at the intersection of engineering and operations, where I worked alongside cross-functional teams to redesign material-handling workflows, analyze production data, and develop workstation concepts that would support the seamless transition to a more automated environment.
I also had the privilege of developing and earning a Green Belt in Design for Six Sigma (DFSS) — a certification that has fundamentally shaped how I approach engineering problems. DFSS trained me to minimize variation and bias in process design, allowing me to build fine-tuned solutions that are statistically validated.

DASION — Software Engineering Intern
In summer 2025, I interned at Dasion as a Software Engineering Intern based in Claremont, California. Dasion is a data-driven company focused on leveraging machine learning to support medical and behavioral research. My role placed me at the intersection of software engineering and applied machine learning, where I worked on developing tools to support emotion recognition in children using medical imaging data.

One of the most exciting aspects of this internship was building an emotion-based music recommender using the Spotify API — a creative application that connected the emotional state detected by our models to curated playlists, demonstrating the real-world potential of the system beyond clinical settings.

HARVEY MUDD COLLEGE — Machine Shop Proctor
The Harvey Mudd Machine Shop serves as a creative space for the 7 Claremont Colleges, welcoming people from all different backgrounds in machining to work on personal projects, class projects, and team projects — allowing for the full spectrum of the creative space to come to life. The shop features both a wooden shop and a metal shop, each equipped with a variety of tools that support everything from early-stage prototyping to precision manufacturing.
As a Machine Shop Proctor, my role is to guide new and existing users on safe practices while assisting with project development for classes. This means being present on the floor, understanding what each person is trying to build, and helping them navigate the right tools, techniques, and processes to get there — safely and effectively.
Beyond day-to-day guidance, I participate in weekly trainings that continuously build my knowledge of machining, tooling, and manufacturing processes. These sessions have deepened my understanding of the machines I work with and made me a more effective resource for the students and makers who rely on the shop.
I also play a direct role in supporting engineering courses at Harvey Mudd, including Introduction to Engineering Design and Manufacturing and Mechanical Design, where I guide students through reading and following process routers and technical drawings to manufacture components to specification — skills that form the foundation of any engineering career.

title: SEM Sample Height Measuring Jig
text:
The final prototype (CALEL), printed in PLA.
  
  
    Summary. In Engineering Design & Manufacturing (E4), our team designed a hand-operated jig that lets Scanning Electron Microscope (SEM) users find the tallest point of a mounted sample without touching it. A rack and pinion raises a laser to the sample's height, and a slew bearing sweeps the beam around it to find the highest peak. The user then reads the height off digital calipers.
    
      Course: E4 Engineering Design & Manufacturing, Fall 2025
      Team: Team BTE
      Client: an SEM research lab, based in Australia
      Budget: $50 limit, $26 spent
      Tools: SolidWorks, 3D printing (PLA), digital calipers

title: SEM Sample Height Measuring Jig
text:
The problem
SEM users had to estimate sample height by eye against a ruler, and then type that number into the microscope. A wrong height can crash a sample into the chamber and damage sensitive detectors, and the client said repairs can take months. The top of each sample also carries a conductive coating only nanometers thick, so anything that touches it can ruin it.

Constraints (hard limits, in priority order)







Constraint
How we met it




Set up in under 30 seconds
10 to 15 seconds on average in testing


Never touch the sample
The bearing’s center hole is 3 mm wider than the platform, so nothing can reach a sample on it


Measure in increments of 1 mm or better
0.39 mm average error, read on calipers accurate to 0.02 mm


Fit a 10 cm holder with seven 26 mm samples
The 100 mm platform takes the largest holder exactly, and smaller ones too


Handle a 50 mm height offset
Measures up to 184 mm


Stay within a $50 project budget
We spent $26





Objectives (what we tried to maximize, in priority order)







Objective
How we judged it




1. Measurement accuracy
People outside the team measured five objects without knowing the true heights. Average error of 0.39 mm scored 4 out of 5 on our rubric


2. Durability
The PLA prototype held up through repeated use by many people. The client can reprint in tougher nylon


3. Replicability
We delivered SolidWorks and STL files so her lab can print it. The non-printed parts are cheap and easy to find


4. Short setup time
10 to 15 seconds to place a sample and reset the bearing


5. User safety
Every edge sanded smooth, non-toxic material, and a wall that blocks the laser from eyes


6. Readable measurement
The digital caliper shows the height as a number

title: SEM Sample Height Measuring Jig
text:
What I was responsible for

Z-axis. I designed the rack-and-pinion mechanism that raises and lowers the laser.
Radial sweep. I designed the slew bearing that rotates the laser around the sample.
Laser system. I worked on the laser and its protective wall, and on the CAD drawings, bill of materials and process router for the final design.

title: SEM Sample Height Measuring Jig
text:
How the design works

  Side view of the known tilt: the bearing is supported by one rack (A) but not the other pillar (B).


The user sets the sample on a 100 mm platform at the center of the base.
A hand crank turns the pinion along the rack and lifts the laser to the sample’s height. A silicone O-ring adds friction so the crank stays put without backlash.
The user turns the slew bearing’s handle to sweep the beam over the whole sample and find the tallest peak. The bearing’s center hole is 3 mm wider than the platform, so it can never hit the sample.
A printed wall opposite the laser catches the beam, which protects eyes and makes the beam easy to see.
The user removes the sample and measures from the platform to the beam’s center with the depth gauge of a digital caliper, reading the height off its display.

title: SEM Sample Height Measuring Jig
text:
Design decisions

Choosing a concept. We generated five alternatives from a morphological chart: a flexible measuring laser, a circular aluminum gauge ring, a micrometer ruler, a LIDAR scanner and an inductive scanner. The LIDAR scanner failed the 30-second setup constraint. The inductive scanner scored highest overall but cost much more, and we asked for a budget increase to test it. The laser design, the lower-cost option, became our prototype.
Material. We printed in PLA because it was free and easy to get, which mattered under a $50 budget. We finished at $26. We recommended nylon to the client for its low friction and wear resistance, and she may have access to it.
Replicability. The client asked for files, not a physical unit, so we delivered SolidWorks and STL packages that her team can print. The non-printed parts are cheap and easy to find, and cost about a third of our E4 budget.
Safety. We sanded every sharp edge, including the cut threaded rod, and the material is non-toxic.

title: SEM Sample Height Measuring Jig
text:
Results

  0.39 mmaverage error across test objects
  10–15 ssetup time, against a 30 s limit
  184 mmmaximum measurable height, against 50 mm needed
  0 contactno part can touch the sample

We had people outside our team follow a one-page instruction sheet to measure five objects of varying height: a PVC pipe, a glue bottle, a plant, a packing peanut and a broken pencil. We did not tell them the true heights. The average error was 0.39 mm, which scored 4 out of 5 on our accuracy rubric and met the client’s 1 mm requirement.

  Residuals (top) and measured vs. actual height (bottom) for the five test objects.

The main flaw is a slight tilt. The bearing was attached to only one rack instead of also being supported by the second pillar, so it tilts a little as it rises. Our test users got the best readings by placing the caliper next to the tallest point, which keeps the tilt from skewing the number. We think the tilt explains most of the remaining error.

title: SEM Sample Height Measuring Jig
text:
What I would change
Add a second rack with a second pinion on a shared rod, so both sides lift equally and the tilt disappears. We also sketched an inductive-sensor design that would stop motorized motion automatically when it senses the conductive sample coating, which would remove human error entirely. We didn’t build it because of time and budget.

  Sketch of the proposed inductive-sensor version.

title: Submersible Robot with Kp Control
text:
The finished submersible ROV.
  
  
    Summary. In Systems Engineering (E79), I built an underwater remotely operated vehicle (ROV) that measures temperature and pressure in lake environments. Its sensor signals are conditioned on a custom PCB and analyzed in LabVIEW. I worked with a partner throughout the semester to get comfortable with the electronics and to apply systems concepts to real hardware that collects real data.
    
      Course: E79 Systems Engineering, Oct – Dec 2025
      Sensors: MCP9701 thermistor, MPX5700ASX pressure gauge
      Electronics: MCP6002 op-amp on an assembled PCB
      Tools: LabVIEW, oscilloscope, DMM, soldering

title: Submersible Robot with Kp Control
text:
What I was responsible for

Partnership. I worked with a partner all semester to build up our understanding of the electronics, from breadboarding to a finished board, and to apply systems concepts to real devices that could gather data.
PCB. I assembled the PCB containing the MCP6002 op-amp that conditions the sensor signals and returns their output voltages.
Soldering and testing. I soldered each circuit and tested it with an oscilloscope and a DMM to verify signal integrity before deployment.
Analysis. I modeled and analyzed the output voltages in LabVIEW to interpret the sensor readings.

title: Submersible Robot with Kp Control
text:
Results
We deployed the ROV at a local lake. Its depth controller used proportional (Kp) control, and the graph below shows the logged depth against the commanded depth over about four minutes of the run.

  Measured depth (blue) vs. desired depth (red) during the lake deployment. The ROV was commanded between about 0.2 m and 1.0 m.

The ROV followed each depth command. It rose to 1.0 m and held it with small oscillations, then dropped back to about 0.2 m, and it repeated this on several cycles.

title: Submersible Robot with Kp Control
text:
What I learned
The project let us take systems-engineering ideas out of the textbook and use them on hardware we built ourselves: sensors, signal conditioning and data analysis, working together as a pair. By the end I was comfortable designing, soldering, testing and debugging the electronics that turn a physical measurement into usable data.

title: Submersible Robot with Kp Control
text:
Why a cost-effective ROV
Underwater ROVs are a cost-effective way to gather environmental data in aquatic settings. The goal was a vehicle robust enough for real lake deployment while still buildable within the limits of a course project.

title: Autonomous Ocean Profiling Robot for Climate Monitoring
text:
The final robot build.
  
  
    Summary. In Experimental Engineering (E80) at Harvey Mudd, our team of four designed, built and deployed an autonomous underwater vehicle that dove to 3 m at Dana Point, California, and measured how UV intensity and temperature change with depth. Both depend on sunlight and matter to marine life: some fish use UV for vision, while UV-B can seriously harm plankton.
    
      Course: E80 Experimental Engineering, Spring 2026
      Team: Ali El Seblani, Carolyn Davis, Keegan Cabrera, Jessica Li
      Sensors: MPX5700 pressure, Murata NXFT15WB473FA2B150 thermistor, GUVA-S12SD UV
      Constraint: $50 budget for sensors
      Controller: Teensy 4.0, 10 Hz logging to SD card

title: Autonomous Ocean Profiling Robot for Climate Monitoring
text:
What I was responsible for

Electrical design. I led the design of the resistance-to-voltage interface for the thermistor and assisted with the voltage-to-voltage interface for the pressure sensor. The team’s sensor interfaces each use a unity-gain buffer and an inverting offset amplifier.
Calibration. I developed the calibration procedures and curves for the pressure and temperature sensors, and the field check of the UV sensor.
Depth control. I developed the C++ depth-control algorithm that sent the robot to each waypoint.
Data analysis. I wrote the MATLAB scripts that read the SD-card logs and produced the depth, temperature and UV plots.
Buoyancy. I helped design and build the frame and ballast so the robot stayed neutrally buoyant in saltwater with minimal tilt.

title: Autonomous Ocean Profiling Robot for Climate Monitoring
text:
Results

  0.5 to 3 mdepth waypoints reached autonomously
  ~46% / mUV decay with depth, UV = 0.273·e−0.762·depth
  0.189 → 0.03UV reading from 0 to 3 m (84% drop)
  18.1 °Csteady temperature, 0.6 °C below the 18.7 °C ground-truth reading

UV intensity fell off exponentially with depth, as Beer-Lambert attenuation predicts, so almost no UV reached 3 m. Temperature stayed essentially constant over the 0 to 3 m range tested. The deployment was on an overcast morning at about 8:30 am, with a surface UV rating near 2.
The robot also had clear limits. At greater depth it lost neutral buoyancy and began to sink, so after its last waypoint it could not resurface by itself. The thermistor was close to the motors, so electromagnetic interference made the temperature trace very noisy. I read temperature only during the 4-second motor stops at each waypoint, when the motors were off.

  Depth vs. desired depth over time. The robot reaches each waypoint.
  UV intensity vs. depth, decaying exponentially.
  Temperature vs. depth. Gaps between motor spikes give the true readings.

title: Autonomous Ocean Profiling Robot for Climate Monitoring
text:
Design decisions

Why UV and temperature. We compared four concepts: a surface vehicle with a UV and temperature heat map, a salinity profiler, a current-and-depth profiler, and a surface vehicle with a tethered AUV. We chose the depth profile of UV and temperature because both come from the sun and it needed only three added sensors, which fit the $50 sensor limit.
Sensor ranges. Each sensor was scaled to 0.3 to 3 V so the Teensy’s 0 to 3.3 V input never clipped, and so each signal used the full range for better resolution. Pressure used a gain of about 10 with inverted output, mapping 0 m to high voltage and 3 m to low.
Calibration. I calibrated depth against voltage with a meter stick in 0.1 m steps, then repeated it at Dana Point because saltwater (about 1020 kg/m³) differs from fresh water. A best-fit line through the 0 to 1 m data gave depth = −1.9 × voltage + 5.17 (depth in meters, voltage in volts). I calibrated the thermistor against a thermometer across 10 to 20 °C.
Stability. A symmetric, rigid frame limited tilt. The electronics box sits high so the center of buoyancy is above the center of mass, and I sized ballast from the buoyancy calculation. Motors sit at least 30 cm from the electronics to cut interference.
Motor mounts. We designed in CAD and 3D printed mounts that hold the two motors steady and an equal distance apart. Where the motors sit mattered as much as how they are held. A motor underneath the electronics box would push water up against it, which adds buoyancy and keeps the robot from diving. Motors near the sensors also induce electromagnetic noise in their signals. So the mounts keep the motors at least 30 cm from the electronics and out of line with the box. We 3D printed the mounts in PLA because printing made them easy to manufacture and let us prototype quickly without adding to our cost.
UV window. A quartz window over the UV sensor keeps the electronics box from absorbing UV.


  
  The motor mount we modeled in CAD and 3D printed.


  Pressure: voltage-to-voltage interface with unity-gain buffer.
  Thermistor: resistance-to-voltage inverting offset amplifier.
  UV: sensor output buffered and offset to the Teensy range.


  Isometric PCB view.
  Top-down PCB view.

title: Autonomous Ocean Profiling Robot for Climate Monitoring
text:
Hand calculations
I sized the robot and its circuits by hand before building anything. Each calculation opens to show the steps.


Stability: keeping the center of buoyancy above the center of mass

Goal. The robot must not tip over underwater, so its center of buoyancy (COB) has to sit above its center of mass (COM). Two design choices make that happen. The electronics box is mostly empty, so the air in it adds a large amount of buoyancy high on the frame, and foam floats on the top PVC raise the COB further. Ballast at the bottom pulls the COM down.
1. Buoyancy of the air-filled electronics box. The box measures 0.15 × 0.13 × 0.08 m, so \(V = 1.56\times10^{-3}\ \text{m}^3\).
\[F_{box} = \rho g V = (997)(9.81)(1.56\times10^{-3}) = 15.26\ \text{N (fresh water)}\]
With saltwater (\(\rho = 1025\) kg/m³) this becomes 15.69 N.
2. Total buoyancy. Add 10 N from the floats on the Lab 1 robot and 5 N for the extra PVC we added, which assumes 1.5 times the PVC of the Lab 1 robot.
\[F_B = 15.26 + 10 + 5 = 30.26\ \text{N (fresh)}\qquad F_B = 15.69 + 10 + 5 = 30.69\ \text{N (salt)}\]
3. Ballast for neutral buoyancy. The robot is neutral when its weight equals \(F_B\). The robot without ballast is about 1 kg, so
\[m_{ballast} = \frac{F_B}{g} - m_{robot} = \frac{30.26}{9.81} - 1 = 2.08\ \text{kg (fresh)}\qquad \frac{30.69}{9.81} - 1 = 2.13\ \text{kg (salt)}\]
4. Center of mass. I split the robot into three levels and estimated each one’s mass and its height above the bottom.

\[COB = \frac{\sum x\,F}{\sum F} = \frac{0(3) + 4(15.26) + 25(5) + 55(7)}{30.26} = 18.87\ \text{cm}\]
Result. The COB is about 12.7 cm above the COM, so any tilt produces a torque that rights the robot. Because the box is empty, I also made sure the buoyancy it adds does not lift the robot out of balance, which is why the ballast sits at the very bottom.



Thermistor: resistance-to-voltage circuit (gain 4.7, Rf = 47 kΩ, Rn1 = 10 kΩ)

Goal. The circuit is an inverting offset amplifier built around the thermistor. It has to take the water temperatures we expected at Dana Point, 10 to 20 °C, and map them onto the Teensy’s usable range of 0.3 to 3 V. Here \(R_t\) is the thermistor’s resistance.



Thermistor interface circuit


1. Thermistor resistance at each end of the range. With \(R_0 = 47\ \text{k}\Omega\) at 25 °C and \(\beta = 4050\):
\[R = R_0\, e^{\beta\left(\frac{1}{T}-\frac{1}{298.15}\right)}\]
\[R_{10^\circ C} = 47\text{k}\cdot e^{4050\left(\frac{1}{283.15}-\frac{1}{298.15}\right)} = 96{,}520\ \Omega\]
\[R_{20^\circ C} = 47\text{k}\cdot e^{4050\left(\frac{1}{293.15}-\frac{1}{298.15}\right)} = 59{,}254\ \Omega\]
2. Expected voltage. I put the thermistor in a voltage divider with \(R_2 = 47\ \text{k}\Omega\) (its resistance at room temperature) and \(V_{in} = 5\) V. The output sits between \(R_t\) and \(R_2\):
\[V_{out} = V_{in}\,\frac{R_2}{R_t + R_2}\]
\[V_{out,10} = 5\cdot\frac{47000}{96520+47000} = 1.637\ \text{V}\qquad V_{out,20} = 5\cdot\frac{47000}{59254+47000} = 2.21\ \text{V}\]
3. Gain. The Teensy’s range is 0.3 to 3 V, so the 0.573 V swing has to grow to 2.7 V:
\[gain = \frac{\Delta V_{out}}{\Delta V_{in}} = \frac{3-0.3}{2.21-1.637} = 4.71\]
The amplifier is inverting, so
\[gain = -\frac{R_f}{R_{n1}} = -4.71\ \Rightarrow\ R_f = 4.71\,R_{n1}\]
I used \(R_f = 47\ \text{k}\Omega\) and \(R_{n1} = 10\ \text{k}\Omega\), which gives 4.7.
4. Offset. The inverting gain flips high and low, so the highest input (20 °C, 2.21 V) becomes the lowest output:
\[2.21\times(-4.71) = -10.41\ \text{V}\]
I want that point to read 0.3 V, so the offset is \(0.3 + 10.41 = 10.71\) V.
5. Offset resistors. The amplifier’s output is
\[V_{out} = \left(1+\frac{R_f}{R_{n1}}\right)\left(\frac{R_g}{R_{p1}+R_g}\right)V_{p1} - \frac{R_f}{R_{n1}}\,V_{in}\]
The first term is the offset, so I solve it for 10.71 V. Let \(V_+ = V_{p1}\frac{R_g}{R_g+R_{p1}}\) be the voltage at the non-inverting input:
\[\left(1+\frac{R_f}{R_{n1}}\right)V_+ = 10.71\ \Rightarrow\ V_+ = \frac{10.71}{5.71} = 1.876\ \text{V}\]
With \(V_{p1} = 5\) V:
\[1.876 = 5\,\frac{R_g}{R_g+R_{p1}}\ \Rightarrow\ R_{p1} = 1.66\,R_g\]
Final values: \(R_g = 10\ \text{k}\Omega\), \(R_{p1} = 16.6\ \text{k}\Omega\), \(R_f = 47\ \text{k}\Omega\), \(R_{n1} = 10\ \text{k}\Omega\).



Pressure sensor: voltage-to-voltage circuit (gain 11, Rf = 110 kΩ, Rn1 = 10 kΩ)

Goal. Turn the pressure sensor’s small voltage change over 0 to 3 m of depth into a signal that fills most of the Teensy’s range. A unity-gain buffer sits in front of the amplifier so the sensor is not loaded.



Pressure sensor interface circuit


1. Sensor output. From the datasheet, with \(V_S = 5\) V, \(P_{atm} = 101.3\) kPa (from a barometer) and \(\rho = 1020\) kg/m³ for seawater:
\[V_{in} = V_S\left(0.0012858\,(P_{atm}+\rho g h) + 0.04\right)\]
At 0 m this is 0.851 V and at 3 m it is 1.044 V, so \(\Delta V_{in} = 0.193\) V.
2. Gain. I want the output to swing 2.0 V (0.5 V to 2.5 V) over that range:
\[|gain| = \frac{\Delta V_{out}}{\Delta V_{in}} = \frac{2.0}{0.193} = 10.36 = \frac{R_f}{R_{n1}}\ \Rightarrow\ R_f = 103.6\ \text{k}\Omega\ \text{for}\ R_{n1} = 10\ \text{k}\Omega\]
The gain is negative, so 0 m reads high and 3 m reads low. Keeping it near 10 limits the error that gain adds.
3. Offset. I place the 0 m reading at 2.2 V, so the 3 m reading lands near 0.2 V:
\[V_{offset} = V_{in}(0)\cdot gain + 2.2 = 0.851(10.36) + 2.2 = 11.02\ \text{V}\]
The offset comes from \((1+G)\,V_+\), so
\[V_+ = \frac{11.02}{1+10.36} = 0.970\ \text{V}\]
4. Offset resistors. With \(V_{p1} = 5\) V and \(R_g = 10\ \text{k}\Omega\):
\[V_+ = 5\,\frac{R_g}{R_g+R_{p1}}\ \Rightarrow\ R_{p1} = 41.5\ \text{k}\Omega\]
5. Built values. The calculation gives \(R_f = 103.6\ \text{k}\Omega\). I built the circuit with \(R_f = 110\ \text{k}\Omega\), which is close to the ideal and gives a slightly higher gain of 11, along with \(R_{n1} = 10\ \text{k}\Omega\), \(R_{p1} = 40\ \text{k}\Omega\) and \(R_g = 10\ \text{k}\Omega\). The output is then \(V_{out} = 12 - 11\,V_{in}\), which is about 2.64 V at 0 m and 0.51 V at 3 m, still well inside the Teensy’s 0.3 to 3 V range.



UV sensor: voltage-to-voltage circuit (gain 2.7, Rf = 27 kΩ, Rn1 = 10 kΩ)

Goal. The sensor outputs \(V = 0.1\times UV\). Dana Point’s UV index could reach about 8, so the sensor output spans 0 to 0.8 V. A unity-gain buffer sits in front of the amplifier, and the circuit places the signal on the Teensy’s range.



UV sensor interface circuit


1. Gain. I want the output to run from 2.8 V at UV 0 down to 0.6 V at UV 8:
\[|gain| = \frac{\Delta V_{out}}{\Delta V_{in}} = \frac{2.8-0.6}{0.8-0} = 2.75 = \frac{R_f}{R_{n1}}\ \Rightarrow\ R_f = 27.5\ \text{k}\Omega\ \text{for}\ R_{n1} = 10\ \text{k}\Omega\]
2. Offset. At UV 0 the sensor voltage is 0, so the output there is the offset itself, 2.8 V:
\[(1+G)\,V_+ = 2.8\ \Rightarrow\ V_+ = \frac{2.8}{1+2.75} = 0.747\ \text{V}\]
3. Offset resistors. With \(V_{p1} = 5\) V and \(R_g = 10\ \text{k}\Omega\):
\[V_+ = 5\,\frac{R_g}{R_g+R_{p1}}\ \Rightarrow\ R_{p1} = 57.0\ \text{k}\Omega\]
4. Built values. I used \(R_f = 27\ \text{k}\Omega\) (gain 2.7), \(R_{n1} = 10\ \text{k}\Omega\), \(R_{p1} = 57\ \text{k}\Omega\) (a 47 kΩ and a 10 kΩ resistor in series) and \(R_g = 10\ \text{k}\Omega\). Those give an actual offset of 2.76 V and \(V_{out} = 2.76 - 2.7\,V_{in}\).

Battery life

The motors draw the most current, and in Lab 0 each motor pulled less than 500 mA. With two motors and a 3300 mAh battery:
\[t = \frac{3300\ \text{mAh}}{2\times 500\ \text{mA}} = 3.3\ \text{hours}\]

title: Autonomous Ocean Profiling Robot for Climate Monitoring
section: Problems and how we handled them
text:
Problems and how we handled them

Motor noise in the temperature signal. Salt water is conductive, so the motors’ electromagnetic interference swamped the thermistor. We programmed a 4-second motor stop at each waypoint and read temperature only during those gaps.
Buoyancy changed with depth. The robot was neutral at the surface but became heavier as pressure rose, so it sank at the last waypoint and could not resurface alone.
Saltwater ballast. The extra density of seawater changed how much ballast we needed, so we trimmed it on site before the dive.

title: Autonomous Ocean Profiling Robot for Climate Monitoring
text:
Deployment
We deployed near the pier at Dana Point harbor. On site we checked waterproofing, trimmed ballast for saltwater and recorded ground-truth readings (18.7 °C, UV rating about 2, 101.3 kPa) before the dive. The robot logged to an SD card, which we analyzed in MATLAB afterward.

  
  Aerial view of the Dana Point harbor. The red dot marks where we deployed, in the water near the pier.

title: Autonomous Ocean Profiling Robot for Climate Monitoring
text:
What I would change
Move the thermistor well away from the motors to remove the noise, and redo the ballast for the pressure at depth so the robot stays neutral and can surface. We would also repeat the dive at other harbor locations and times of day to compare UV and temperature.
